H1.text: A gate swings about its hinge. A wheel turns on its axle. A pendulum swings from near its top.

H2.text: Same kind of object, a different axis, a different moment of inertia.

H3.text: Diya spins a coin flat. Then on its edge. Then on a pin through its rim.

H4.text: One coin, three spins, three answers. Must she start from scratch each time?

H5.text: No. Two shortcuts do it. The theorems of perpendicular and parallel axes.

P1.text: Note: these theorems are not in the current NCERT book. They are in the ISC, JEE and NEET syllabus.

P2.text: The perpendicular axes theorem works only for flat bodies, like a coin or a plate.

P3.text: The parallel axes theorem works for any body, as long as one axis passes through the centre of mass.

G1.text: First, perpendicular axes. Lay the coin flat. Draw x and y in its plane, and z straight up through its centre.

G2.text: A bit of the coin sits at x and y. Its distance from the z axis is r, and r squared equals x squared plus y squared.

G3.text: Multiply by m and add every bit. The sum of m r squared splits in two.

G4.text: Those are I about x, and I about y. So I z equals I x plus I y.

G5.text: For the coin, I z is half M R squared, and by symmetry I x equals I y. So each is a quarter M R squared: the coin spun on its edge.

G6.text: Now you try. A ring has I equal to M R squared about its central axis. About a diameter, is it M R squared, or half? Pause and decide.

G7.text: Half M R squared! The two diameters share the total equally.

S1.text: Now parallel axes, on our motion notebook. A two kilogram disc, radius point two metres, spinning about its centre. I is point zero four.

S2.text: Move the axis point one metres away from the centre. Now the centre of the disc goes round in a circle too.

S4.text: The motion has two parts. The centre goes round the axis, like a mass M at distance d. That adds M d squared.

S5.text: And it still turns about its own centre, keeping I c m. Total: point zero six.

S6.text: Slide the axis to the rim. d is point two, M d squared is point zero eight, and I is point one two. Three times as much.

S7.text: On the graph, I against d squared is a straight line. It starts at I c m, and its slope is the mass.

D1.text: Why does this work? Step by step.

D2.text: Step one. Measure each bit from the centre of mass with r. From the new axis, its distance is r plus d.

D3.text: Step two. Square it and add. You get the sum of m r squared, plus two d times the sum of m r, plus M d squared.

D4.text: Step three. Measured from the centre of mass, the sum of m r is zero. So the middle part vanishes.

D5.text: Step four. What is left is I c m plus M d squared.

T1.text: Remember this. Parallel axes: I equals I c m plus M d squared. Perpendicular axes: I z equals I x plus I y, for flat bodies only.

K1.text: Side by side. A thin rod about its middle has M L squared over twelve.

K2.text: Shift the axis to its end, half a length away. Add M times L over two, squared. That is M L squared over three, four times bigger. That is why the ruler was hard to spin by its end.

K3.text: Now you try. Of all the parallel axes through a body, which one gives the smallest moment of inertia? Pause and decide.

K4.text: The one through the centre of mass! Any other axis adds M d squared on top.

W2.text: A two kilogram disc of radius point two metres. Find I about a tangent in its plane.

W3.text: First, perpendicular axes. About a diameter, I is half of point zero four. Point zero two.

W4.text: The tangent is parallel to it, a distance R away. Add M R squared: two times point zero four. Point zero eight.

W5.text: So I is point zero two plus point zero eight. Point one kilogram metre squared.

X2.text: Many students add M d squared between any two parallel axes.

X3.text: But one axis must pass through the centre of mass. Between two other axes, go through the centre of mass first.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In finding I about an edge, a corner or a tangent, using one or both theorems.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A uniform square plate, mass M, side a, has I equal to M a squared over six about its central axis at right angles to it. Find I about a diagonal. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. M a squared over twelve.

A2.text: The two diagonals cross at right angles in the plate, through its centre.

A3.text: So by perpendicular axes, the two diagonal values add up to M a squared over six.

A4.text: By symmetry they are equal. So each is M a squared over twelve.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. Why must one of the axes pass through the centre of mass?

Y3.text: Two. Why does the perpendicular axes theorem work only for flat bodies?

Y4.text: Three. Which parallel axis gives the smallest moment of inertia, and why?

N1.text: Next time: a potter keeps a heavy wheel turning with one foot. How much work does each push do? Torque, work and rotational kinetic energy.
